title: Sustainable Textile Colouring: Using Pinus pinaster Aiton Waste for Natural Dyes and Reducing the Carbon Footprint
content: This academic article presents a comprehensive analysis of the emissions associated with using Pinus pinaster Aiton pine cone waste to produce natural textile dyes, offering a sustainable alternative to synthetic dyes that aligns with decarbonisation objectives and circular economy principles. The main objective was to assess the potential for reducing carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂ eq) emissions by replacing synthetic dyes with natural dyes derived from residual biomass, applying a Life Cycle Analysis (LCA) framework. The methodology included the experimental extraction of dyes, followed by a characterisation of the pine cone waste, the resulting extract and the pine cone waste, along with a comparative assessment of emissions between the natural and synthetic dye production processes. The study revealed that the pine cone waste had a fixed carbon content of (75.6%), consistent with values for woody waste such as bark and pine cones, which can vary between 75% and 78%, reinforcing previous research. While the extract had a lower fixed carbon content (0.4%), modest compared to other botanical extracts used in the production of textile dyes, the pine cone residue had a moderate fixed carbon content of (1.7%,) showing potential for biochar and adsorption applications. The life cycle analysis revealed that electricity consumption accounted for (85.8%) of emissions during the extraction process, highlighting the importance of increasing energy efficiency. Ultimately, this study emphasises that the production of natural textile dyes from pine cone waste provides substantial environmental advantages, reinforces circular economy practices and offers a viable strategy for sustainability in the textile sector.
